scenes.text: A shop in Chandigarh advertises '20% off, then another 20% off at the counter!' Simran's friend says that's 40% off.
Simran, preparing for CUET, calculates: it's 36% off.
Percentages hide traps; one formula reveals them.

steps.title: About this material
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide (information bulletin) for the current sections, syllabus and pattern.

steps.title: Percentages
steps.body:
- x% of y = xy/100. Percentage change = (change/original) × 100.
- **Successive changes** a% and b%: net = a + b + ab/100. Two 20% discounts: −20 − 20 + 400/100 = **−36%**. A 20% rise then a 20% fall: +20 − 20 − 4 = **−4%**.
- If A is 25% more than B, B is 20% less than A (25/125 = 20%).

steps.title: Ratios and averages
steps.body:
- Divide ₹1,200 in ratio 2 : 3 : 5 ⇒ 240, 360, 600.
- Average = sum/count. If the average of 5 numbers is 20 and one number 30 is removed, the new average = (100 − 30)/4 = **17.5**.
- Weighted average: 30 students averaging 60 and 20 averaging 70 ⇒ (1800 + 1400)/50 = **64**.

steps.title: Speed, time, work
steps.body:
- Speed = distance/time; 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s.
- Average speed for equal distances at u and v: **2uv/(u + v)** (not (u + v)/2). 40 and 60 km/h ⇒ 48 km/h.
- Work: if A takes a days and B takes b days, together ab/(a + b) days. 10 and 15 ⇒ **6 days**.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Adding successive percentages directly.
- Averaging speeds instead of using total distance/total time.
- Using the new value as the base in percentage change.

lessons.title: Logical reasoning: series, coding, syllogisms, relations

scenes.text: On the bus to her Kolkata college coaching, Riddhi solves a puzzle a day on her phone.
Today: 'If CAT is coded as DBU, how is DOG coded?' She grins—each letter moves one step.
Reasoning questions reward patterns you've seen before.

steps.title: Series
steps.body:
Look for differences, ratios, squares/cubes, or alternating patterns.
- 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ? ⇒ differences 4, 6, 8, 10 ⇒ next **42** (n(n + 1)).
- 3, 9, 27, 81 ⇒ ×3 ⇒ **243**.
- 1, 4, 9, 16, ? ⇒ squares ⇒ **25**.
- Letter series: A, C, F, J, ? ⇒ gaps 2, 3, 4, 5 ⇒ **O**.

steps.title: Coding–decoding and relations
steps.body:
- CAT → DBU (+1 each) ⇒ DOG → **EPH**.
- Alphabet positions: A = 1 … Z = 26; opposite pairs add to 27 (A–Z, B–Y).
- Blood relations: draw a family tree with symbols (+ male, − female, = married). 'Pointing to a man, Riya says, "His mother is the only daughter of my mother."' ⇒ his mother is Riya herself ⇒ the man is Riya's **son**.

steps.title: Syllogisms with Venn diagrams
steps.body:
'All A are B. Some B are C.' Does 'Some A are C' follow? Draw it: A inside B; C overlaps B but may miss A ⇒ **does not necessarily follow**.

'All A are B. All B are C.' ⇒ 'All A are C' **follows**.

Only conclusions true in **every** possible diagram follow.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Using real-world knowledge in syllogisms—only the given statements count.
- Assuming gender from names in blood-relation questions unless stated.
- Stopping at the first pattern without checking all terms.

steps.title: Active reading
steps.body:
- First pass: find the **main idea**, the author's **tone** (critical, neutral, optimistic) and the **structure** (problem → cause → solution).
- Note signal words: *however, therefore, although, in contrast*—they mark turns in the argument.
- Answer from the passage, not from your general knowledge.

steps.title: Question types
steps.body:
- **Main idea**: the option that covers the whole passage, not one paragraph.
- **Detail**: locate the exact line.
- **Inference**: what must be true given the text—small, safe steps only.
- **Vocabulary in context**: replace the word with each option and reread the sentence.
- **Tone**: look at adjectives and verbs the author chooses.

steps.title: Elimination in action
steps.body:
Passage: 'Although solar power is now cheaper than coal in many regions, grid storage remains a bottleneck.'

Which inference follows? (a) Coal is obsolete. (b) Cheap generation alone does not solve reliability. (c) Solar is expensive everywhere. (d) Storage is solved.

Only **(b)** is supported. (a) is too extreme; (c) contradicts; (d) contradicts.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Extreme words (always, never, completely) are often wrong in inference options.
- Options that are true in real life but not stated in the passage.
- Choosing an option that matches only part of the passage for a 'main idea' question.

quiz.why: The answer is "covers the whole passage". Reason: It summarises the passage. The other choices, such as "repeats the title only" and "covers one detail", do not fit the question.

quiz.why: The answer is "supported by the passage". Reason: Grounded in the text. The other choices, such as "possibly true" and "the longest option", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Indian polity: the Constitution at work

scenes.text: On 26 November—Constitution Day—Deepa, a working engineer in Bengaluru preparing for the civil services, reads the Preamble aloud with her study group.
Her friend Iqbal asks: 'Why were "socialist" and "secular" not in the original Preamble?'
Answering takes them through amendments, the basic structure and the balance of power in India.

steps.title: About this material
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide (notification) for the current scheme and syllabus. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Making of the Constitution
steps.body:
- The Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946; Dr Rajendra Prasad was its President; Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.
- The Constitution was **adopted on 26 November 1949** and **came into force on 26 January 1950**.
- The Preamble declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic. The words **socialist**, **secular** and **integrity** were added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**.

steps.title: Rights, principles and duties
steps.body:
- **Fundamental Rights**: Part III (Articles 12–35), justiciable. Article 14 equality before law; 19 freedoms; 21 life and personal liberty; 21A right to education (86th Amendment, 2002); **Article 32** right to constitutional remedies (called by Ambedkar the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution).
- The right to property was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment (1978); it is now a constitutional right under Article 300A.
- **Directive Principles**: Part IV (Articles 36–51), non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.
- **Fundamental Duties**: Article 51A (Part IVA), added by the 42nd Amendment on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation; the 11th duty was added by the 86th Amendment.

steps.title: Institutions and key articles
steps.body:
- Amendment procedure: **Article 368**. The **basic structure** doctrine came from *Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala* (1973): Parliament cannot destroy the Constitution's basic features.
- Money Bill: **Article 110**; the Speaker certifies it; the Rajya Sabha can only delay it for 14 days.
- Emergencies: **352** (national), **356** (failure of constitutional machinery in a state), **360** (financial).
- Election Commission: **Article 324**; Finance Commission: **Article 280**; CAG: **Article 148**.
- Local government: **73rd** (panchayats) and **74th** (municipalities) Amendments, 1992.
- The President is elected by an electoral college of elected MPs and elected MLAs (including those of Delhi and Puducherry); the Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Fundamental Duties are not enforceable in court the way Fundamental Rights are.
- The basic structure doctrine is judge-made, not written in the text.
- Don't confuse Article 356 (state emergency/President's Rule) with Article 352 (national emergency).

scenes.text: At the National Museum in New Delhi, retired teacher Mr Sinha guides his grandson Aakash, a civil services aspirant, past Harappan seals and a Mauryan pillar capital.
'Don't memorise dates as a list,' he says. 'Hang them on a story: cause, event, consequence.'
They end in the freedom-struggle gallery.

steps.title: Ancient and medieval anchors
steps.body:
- **Harappan civilisation**: Harappa excavated in 1921 and Mohenjo-daro in 1922; planned cities, drainage, standardised weights; script still undeciphered.
- **Mauryas**: Chandragupta Maurya (c. 321 BCE); **Ashoka**'s Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE) and his edicts on dhamma.
- **Guptas** (c. 4th–6th century CE): advances in mathematics, astronomy and art.
- **Delhi Sultanate** (from 1206) and the **Mughals**: Babur won the First Battle of Panipat in **1526**; Akbar's administration (mansabdari).

steps.title: Colonial rule and early nationalism
steps.body:
- The **Revolt of 1857** began at Meerut on 10 May 1857; afterwards the Crown took over from the East India Company (1858).
- The **Indian National Congress** was founded in **1885** (first session at Bombay).
- **Partition of Bengal** (1905) under Curzon ⇒ the Swadeshi movement; the partition was annulled in 1911.

steps.title: The Gandhian phase
steps.body:
- Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915; **Champaran Satyagraha** (1917).
- **Jallianwala Bagh massacre**: 13 April 1919, Amritsar.
- **Non-Cooperation Movement** (1920), withdrawn after **Chauri Chaura** (February 1922).
- **Salt March** to Dandi (March–April 1930) began the Civil Disobedience Movement.
- **Quit India Movement**: launched 8 August 1942 ('Do or Die').
- **Independence**: 15 August 1947, with Partition.

steps.title: How to study history for prelims
steps.body: Build one-page timelines per era; link each event to a cause and a consequence; note leaders, places and the exact name of each movement. Use NCERT textbooks for the base, then one standard reference for modern India.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Confusing Non-Cooperation (1920–22) with Civil Disobedience (1930–34).
- Placing the Partition of Bengal after the INC's founding incorrectly—1885 comes first, then 1905.
- Mixing up Champaran (indigo, 1917) and Kheda (peasant revenue, 1918).

lessons.title: Indian geography: relief, rivers, monsoon, soils

scenes.text: Neeraj takes a train from Mumbai to Guwahati. He crosses the Western Ghats, the Deccan plateau's black soils, the Ganga plains and the Brahmaputra.
He marks each region on a blank map in his notebook.
By the end, India's geography is a story he has travelled, not a list.

steps.title: Location and relief
steps.body:
- India covers about 2.4% of the world's land area.
- The **Tropic of Cancer** crosses eight states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.
- Indian Standard Time is based on **82°30′ E**.
- Physiographic divisions: Himalayas, northern plains, peninsular plateau, Indian desert, coastal plains, islands.

steps.title: Rivers
steps.body:
- **Himalayan rivers** (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra systems) are perennial—fed by snow and rain.
- **Peninsular rivers** are mostly rain-fed and seasonal. Most flow east into the Bay of Bengal (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri), forming deltas.
- **Narmada** and **Tapi** flow west into the Arabian Sea through rift valleys and form estuaries.

steps.title: Monsoon and soils
steps.body:
- The south-west monsoon usually reaches Kerala around the start of June and covers most of India by mid-July; it withdraws in September–October.
- The Tamil Nadu coast receives much of its rain in October–December from the north-east/retreating monsoon.
- Mawsynram and Cherrapunji (Meghalaya) are among the wettest places on Earth.
- Soils: **alluvial** (most widespread, plains), **black/regur** (Deccan, good for cotton, retains moisture), **red** (iron-rich), **laterite** (heavy rain, leaching), **arid** and **mountain** soils.

steps.title: Map practice
steps.body: Keep a blank outline map. Each week, add rivers, passes, national parks and places in the news. Map-based questions are easier when you've drawn the map yourself.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Assuming all peninsular rivers form deltas (Narmada and Tapi form estuaries).
- Thinking the whole of India gets its rain mainly in June–September (Tamil Nadu is an exception).
- Forgetting Tripura and Mizoram in the Tropic of Cancer list.

scenes.text: Vegetable prices rise in Pune. Aspirant Megha's mother asks why the RBI raised interest rates—'Won't that make loans costlier?'
Megha explains inflation targeting, repo rates and why fiscal and monetary policy sometimes pull in different directions.
Economics, she realises, is in every kitchen.

steps.title: Growth and inflation
steps.body:
- **GDP**: value of final goods and services produced within the country; real GDP removes price effects.
- **Inflation**: general rise in prices. India's RBI follows **flexible inflation targeting**: CPI inflation of **4% with a band of ±2%**, with policy set by a six-member **Monetary Policy Committee**.
- Wholesale Price Index (WPI) and Consumer Price Index (CPI) measure different baskets.

steps.title: Monetary and fiscal policy
steps.body:
- **Monetary** (RBI): repo rate, CRR, SLR, open market operations. Higher repo ⇒ costlier credit ⇒ lower demand ⇒ lower inflation.
- **Fiscal** (government): taxes and spending. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts).
- RBI was established on 1 April 1935 and nationalised in 1949.

steps.title: Landmarks
steps.body:
- Five-Year Plans began in 1951; the Planning Commission was replaced by **NITI Aayog** on 1 January 2015.
- **1991 reforms**: liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation (LPG).

steps.title: Profit, loss and discounts
steps.body:
- Profit % = (SP − CP)/CP × 100.
- An item costing ₹800 is marked up 25% (₹1,000) and sold at 10% discount ⇒ SP = ₹900 ⇒ profit **12.5%**.
- Selling two items at the same price, one at x% profit and one at x% loss ⇒ overall **loss of x²/100 %**.

steps.title: Time–speed–distance and work
steps.body:
- Relative speed: same direction subtract, opposite add. Trains of 150 m and 100 m at 50 and 40 km/h in opposite directions cross in 250 m/(90 × 5/18 m/s) = 250/25 = **10 s**.
- Boats: downstream = b + s, upstream = b − s.
- Work: A in 10 days, B in 15 ⇒ together 6 days. With pipes, filling is +, emptying is −.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Taking percentage discount on cost price instead of marked price.
- Forgetting to convert units in TSD.
- Assuming CI and SI are equal after 1 year—they are (for annual compounding), but not after.

scenes.text: In a mock, Fatima sees: 'Find the unit digit of 7²⁰²³.' She can't compute 7²⁰²³—and doesn't need to.
Powers of 7 end in 7, 9, 3, 1 and then repeat.
Cycles, remainders and factor tricks make huge numbers small.

steps.title: Unit digits and remainders
steps.body:
- Unit digit cycle of 7: 7, 9, 3, 1 (length 4). 2023 mod 4 = 3 ⇒ unit digit of 7²⁰²³ = **3**.
- Remainder of 2¹⁰ ÷ 7: 2³ = 8 ≡ 1 (mod 7) ⇒ 2⁹ ≡ 1 ⇒ 2¹⁰ ≡ **2**.
- Remainder of a sum/product = remainder of the sum/product of remainders.

steps.title: HCF, LCM and factors
steps.body:
- HCF × LCM = product of two numbers. If HCF = 6 and LCM = 72 and one number is 18, the other is 6 × 72/18 = **24**.
- Number of factors of N = p^a q^b r^c is (a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1). 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5 ⇒ 4 × 3 × 2 = **24 factors**.
- Divisibility: by 3 or 9 via digit sum; by 11 via alternating digit sum.

steps.title: Algebra essentials
steps.body:
- Linear equations: 2 apples + 3 bananas = ₹40; 3 apples + 2 bananas = ₹35 ⇒ adding: 5(a + b) = 75 ⇒ a + b = 15; subtracting: b − a = 5 ⇒ a = 5, b = 10.
- Quadratics: sum and product of roots.
- Inequalities: multiplying by a negative number flips the sign.
- AP sum Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n − 1)d]; GP sum a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1).

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- For unit digits, when the exponent is a multiple of the cycle length, use the last element of the cycle (e.g., 7⁴ ends in 1).
- 1 is neither prime nor composite.
- Forgetting to flip an inequality when dividing by a negative.

steps.title: Passage mapping
steps.body:
- After each paragraph, write a 3–5 word summary (P1: problem; P2: old view; P3: author disagrees).
- Identify the **author's position** versus views the author reports.
- Note tone words (sceptical, cautiously optimistic, dismissive).

steps.title: Option elimination
steps.body:
Eliminate options that are:
- **Out of scope** (introduce new ideas),
- **Extreme** (always, never, entirely),
- **Distorted** (twist a detail),
- **True but irrelevant** to the question asked.
Choose the option you can defend with a line from the passage.

steps.title: Verbal reasoning items
steps.body:
- **Para-jumbles**: find the opening (introduces a topic without pronouns referring back), then link pairs via pronouns, connectors and chronology.
- **Odd sentence out**: find the sentence that breaks the paragraph's theme even if it shares keywords.
- **Summary**: the option that captures the core argument without extra detail or new claims.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Picking an option because it repeats words from the passage.
- Treating a view the author reports as the author's own.
- Spending too long on one hard passage—sometimes skipping a passage is the right call.

scenes.text: A DILR set: five friends each live in a different city and like a different sport. Ten clues. Aarti tries to hold it all in her head and fails.

steps.title: Set selection
steps.body:
- Spend the first few minutes scanning all sets; pick the ones with clear structure and fewer conditional clues.
- A set you can finish completely is worth more than three half-done sets.

steps.title: Grid method for arrangements
steps.body:
- Make a table (people × attributes). Mark ✔ and ✕.
- Start with **definite** clues ('A lives in Delhi'), then **negative** ('B is not in Mumbai'), then **conditional** ('if C plays chess…').
- For seating: fix one person's position; in circular arrangements, 'immediate left' depends on facing direction—draw it.

steps.title: DI quick maths
steps.body:
- Percentage change: (new − old)/old.
- Approximate smartly: 487/1,213 ≈ 0.40.
- Ratios from pie charts: angle/360 × total.
- Growth comparisons: if A grows from 40 to 50 (25%) and B from 80 to 96 (20%), A grew faster in percentage terms even though B grew more in absolute terms.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Assuming 'left' and 'right' without fixing the facing direction.
- Confusing absolute and percentage growth.
- Forcing a solution when the set allows multiple cases—track cases separately.

steps.title: Text completion and sentence equivalence
steps.body:
- Cover the options; read the sentence; predict your own word from **clue words** and **signal words** (although, because, despite, moreover).
- Then match your prediction to the options.
- **Sentence equivalence** asks for two words that give the sentence the same meaning—look for a pair of near-synonyms that both fit.

Example: 'Although the critic's review was ____, the director found it helpful.' 'Although' signals contrast with 'helpful' ⇒ a negative word like *harsh* or *scathing*.

steps.title: Reading comprehension
steps.body: Same principles as any RC: identify the main point and the author's attitude; answer from the text; eliminate extreme or out-of-scope options. Some questions ask you to select all correct options or to select a sentence in the passage.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Choosing a 'hard-sounding' word without checking the logic.
- In sentence equivalence, picking two synonyms that don't fit the sentence.
- Learning word lists without example sentences.

lessons.title: GRE quant: quantitative comparison and data

story.title: The zero that broke the rule

scenes.text: In a practice question, Arjun compares x² and x. He picks 'x² is greater'—and is wrong.
His tutor asks: 'What if x = ½? What if x = 0? What if x is negative?'
Testing special numbers is the heart of quantitative comparison.

steps.title: Quantitative comparison (QC)
steps.body:
You compare Quantity A and Quantity B. Choices: A is greater; B is greater; they are equal; the relationship **cannot be determined** from the information given.

Strategy: test numbers from different categories—**positive, negative, zero, fractions between 0 and 1, large numbers, integers vs non-integers**. If you find two cases giving different relationships, the answer is 'cannot be determined'.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Quantity A: x². Quantity B: x. (No other information.)
- x = 2: A = 4 > B = 2.
- x = ½: A = ¼ < B = ½.
Different results ⇒ **cannot be determined**.

If told x > 1, then A is always greater.

steps.title: Data interpretation basics
steps.body:
- Read titles, units and scales first.
- Estimate before calculating; GRE provides an on-screen calculator, but estimation is often faster.
- Percent of a total vs percent change are different—read which is asked.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Assuming variables are positive integers.
- Assuming figures are drawn to scale unless stated.
- Doing long calculations when simplifying both quantities would be faster.

activity.prompt: For Quantity A = x² and Quantity B = x, which test value gives which result?

quiz.why: The answer is "B greater". Reason: For x > 1, 1/x < 1 < x. The other choices, such as "Cannot be determined" and "A greater", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: If two test values give different relationships, the answer is
quiz.why: The answer is "cannot be determined". Reason: No single relationship holds. The other choices, such as "A greater" and "equal", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A good set of test numbers includes
quiz.why: The answer is "positives, negatives, zero and fractions". Reason: Different categories reveal different behaviour. The other choices, such as "only 1, 2, 3" and "only large numbers", do not fit the question.

quiz.why: The answer is "Cannot be determined". Reason: A is 1 or −1 depending on n. The other choices, such as "Equal" and "A greater", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: GMAT: critical reasoning and data sufficiency

scenes.text: Product manager Aisha in Gurugram is preparing for business school abroad. Data sufficiency questions confuse her: 'You don't want the answer?'
Her mentor explains: 'Only decide whether you could find it. Like a manager deciding if a report has enough data.'

steps.title: About this material
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current format. In the current GMAT format, sections cover Quantitative Reasoning, Verbal Reasoning and Data Insights; data sufficiency questions appear in Data Insights.

steps.title: Critical reasoning
steps.body:
Find the **conclusion**, the **evidence**, and the **gap (assumption)** between them.
- **Assumption**: what must be true for the argument to hold. Negation test: if negating an option destroys the argument, it's the assumption.
- **Strengthen/weaken**: options that close or widen the gap.
- Example: 'Sales rose after the ad campaign, so the campaign caused the rise.' Weakener: 'A competitor shut down the same month.'

steps.title: Data sufficiency (DS)
steps.body:
A question plus two statements. Standard answer choices:
- (A) Statement 1 alone is sufficient, 2 alone is not.
- (B) Statement 2 alone is sufficient, 1 alone is not.
- (C) Both together are sufficient, neither alone.
- (D) Each alone is sufficient.
- (E) Not sufficient even together.
Evaluate each statement **alone** first, then together. For yes/no questions, a statement is sufficient if it gives a definite yes or a definite no.

steps.title: Worked DS example
steps.body:
Is x > 0? (1) x² = 9. (2) x³ = 27.
- (1): x = 3 or −3 ⇒ not sufficient.
- (2): x = 3 ⇒ sufficient.
Answer: **(B)**.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Solving fully when you only need to know if you *could*.
- Carrying information from statement 1 into your evaluation of statement 2 alone.
- In CR, choosing an option that's true but doesn't affect the argument.

lessons.title: How memory works: study smarter

scenes.text: Mira, 15, in Kochi, highlights her history textbook in five colours. It looks beautiful. A week later, she remembers little.
Her older brother, a medical student, quizzes himself with flashcards and blank-page recall every night.
Same hours, very different results. The difference is how memory actually works.

steps.title: Three evidence-based techniques
steps.body:
- **Active recall (retrieval practice)**: test yourself—close the book and write what you remember; use flashcards and past questions. Retrieval strengthens memory far more than re-reading.
- **Spaced repetition**: review after increasing gaps (e.g., 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 1 month). Cramming fades fast.
- **Interleaving**: mix different topics or problem types in one practice session, so you learn to choose the right method.

steps.title: Sleep and memory
steps.body: Sleep helps consolidate what you learned during the day. Pulling all-nighters before exams usually lowers performance. Teens generally need about 8–10 hours; adults about 7–9.

steps.title: Make it stick
steps.body:
- Explain a concept aloud as if teaching a younger student (the 'teach-back' method).
- Draw diagrams from memory.
- Connect new facts to things you already know (stories, examples).

steps.title: Myths
steps.body:
- 'Re-reading many times is the best way.' It feels familiar but builds weak memory.
- 'Highlighting equals learning.' Only if you then test yourself.
- 'Multitasking with phone notifications is fine.' Switching attention costs focus and time.

statements.s: Testing yourself is more effective than re-reading.
Cramming the night before is the best way to remember for months.
statements.why: Spacing works better for long-term memory.

statements.s: Sleep helps consolidate learning.
Highlighting alone is a powerful study method.
statements.why: It is weak unless combined with active recall.

statements.s: Mixing problem types in practice can help you pick the right method in exams.

lessons.title: Time management that survives real life

scenes.text: Farhan, 17, in Hyderabad, makes a 14-hour study timetable. By Wednesday he's exhausted and abandons it.
His cousin suggests a realistic plan: focused 25-minute blocks, short breaks and three priorities per day.
He studies fewer hours—and gets more done.

steps.title: Plan the week, then the day
steps.body:
- Weekly: list chapters, mocks and revision slots; leave buffer time.
- Daily: choose **three priorities** (the most important tasks) and do them first.
- Use the **Eisenhower matrix**: urgent/important first; important but not urgent gets scheduled; urgent but unimportant is minimised; neither is dropped.

steps.title: Focus blocks
steps.body:
- **Pomodoro**: 25 minutes focused work + 5 minutes break; a longer break after four rounds. Adjust (e.g., 50/10) as your focus grows.
- Phone in another room or on 'do not disturb'.
- Start with a two-minute task to beat procrastination.

steps.title: Balance
steps.body: Exercise, meals, family time and sleep are not 'wasted' time—they keep your brain working. Plan them in.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Over-ambitious timetables that collapse by day three.
- Measuring hours instead of tasks completed.
- Saving all revision for the last week.

She remembers her routine: read the whole paper, mark easy questions, start with one she's sure of.

steps.title: A simple routine
steps.body:
1. Read instructions and the whole paper (use reading time if given).
2. Mark questions: ✔ easy, ○ medium, ✕ hard.
3. Start with an easy one to build calm.
4. Budget time by marks (e.g., a 5-mark question gets roughly 5/total of the time).
5. Keep 10 minutes at the end to review.

steps.title: Answer-writing tips
steps.body:
- Underline keywords in the question (explain, compare, calculate).
- For long answers: brief intro, key points with headings, diagram if useful, short conclusion.
- In numericals: write the formula, substitute with units, box the answer.
- If stuck, write what you know—partial credit is often possible in written exams.

steps.title: Guessing in MCQ exams with negative marking
steps.body: With +4 for correct and −1 for wrong on 4 options, a blind guess has expected value +0.25; after eliminating two options, +1.5. Guess only after eliminating options, and always check the actual marking scheme of your exam.

lessons.title: Exam anxiety and fear of failure

scenes.text: The night before his exam, Rehan, 15, in Srinagar, can't sleep. His chest feels tight and he keeps thinking, 'What if I fail?'
His mother sits with him. Together they try slow breathing and write his worries on paper.
He sleeps. The next day, he still feels nervous—but it no longer controls him.

steps.title: What anxiety is
steps.body: Anxiety is the body's alarm system (fight-or-flight): fast heartbeat, tight chest, sweaty palms, racing thoughts. A little helps you focus; too much blocks memory. It is common and it is treatable—not a weakness.

steps.title: Tools that help
steps.body:
- **Breathing**: slow breaths with a longer out-breath, or box breathing (4-4-4-4).
- **Write it down**: spending 10 minutes writing worries before an exam can reduce their grip.
- **Reframe**: 'My heart is racing because my body is getting ready' instead of 'I'm panicking'.
- **Prepare**: practice under exam-like conditions makes the real thing feel familiar.
- **Body basics**: sleep, food, water, a short walk.

steps.title: Fear of failure
steps.body: One exam is one event, not your whole life. Many successful people failed exams, changed paths or tried again. Ask: 'What is one thing I can do today?' rather than 'What if everything goes wrong?'

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: Talk to someone if anxiety stops you sleeping, eating or studying for days, if you feel hopeless, or if you have panic attacks. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, tell someone right away—a parent, teacher, counsellor or doctor—or call **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7), **1098** (Childline, for under-18s) or **112** in an emergency. The Mann (wellbeing) school has more courses on stress, panic and self-care.

lessons.title: Mechanics: picking the right conservation law

scenes.text: In a Kota mock test, Arjun spends 40 minutes on one mechanics problem using forces, drawing six free-body diagrams. He gets it right—and runs out of time for ten others.
His mentor, Ms Iyer, solves the same problem in four lines with energy conservation.
'In JEE,' she says, 'the first skill is choosing the method. Then speed comes free.'

steps.title: About this material
steps.body:
Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.

Problems here are written in the style of JEE Main and Advanced; difficulty is marked in the exam.

steps.title: Method chooser
steps.body:
- Need **speed at a position**, forces are conservative ⇒ **energy**.
- **Collision / explosion / sudden jerk** (no external impulse) ⇒ **momentum**.
- Need **acceleration or tension** ⇒ **forces (FBD)**.
- Rotation about a fixed axis, no external torque ⇒ **angular momentum**.
- Always finish with a units check and a limiting case (m → 0, θ → 0).

steps.title: Problem 1: block on table pulled by hanging mass
steps.body:
A 2 kg block on a smooth table is tied by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 3 kg mass (g = 10 m/s²). Find a and T.

System along the string: 3g = (2 + 3)a ⇒ **a = 6 m/s²**. For the 2 kg block: **T = 2 × 6 = 12 N**. Check: hanging block 30 − 12 = 3 × 6 ✔.

steps.title: Problem 2: ballistic pendulum
steps.body:
A 10 g bullet at 400 m/s embeds in a 2 kg block hanging from a string. How high does the block rise?

- Collision (momentum): 0.01 × 400 = 2.01 V ⇒ V ≈ 1.99 m/s.
- After collision (energy): h = V²/2g ≈ 3.96/20 ≈ **0.198 m ≈ 20 cm**.

Trap: using energy conservation *during* the collision—KE is lost in a perfectly inelastic collision (here > 99% of it!).

steps.title: Problem 3: falling rod
steps.body:
A uniform rod of length L, pivoted at one end, is released from horizontal. Find its angular speed when vertical and the speed of its free end.

Energy: the centre of mass falls L/2: mg(L/2) = ½(mL²/3)ω² ⇒ **ω = √(3g/L)**; tip speed v = ωL = **√(3gL)**—faster than a freely falling stone dropped through L (√(2gL))! The rod's rotation 'whips' the tip.

steps.title: Problem 4: spring stop
steps.body:
A 1 kg block at 2 m/s hits a spring (k = 100 N/m) on a smooth floor. Maximum compression?

½mv² = ½kx² ⇒ x = v√(m/k) = 2 × 0.1 = **0.2 m**. With friction μ = 0.1 the equation becomes ½mv² = ½kx² + μmgx ⇒ 2 = 50x² + x ⇒ x ≈ 0.19 m.

steps.title: Traps examiners love
steps.body:
- Pseudo-forces: only in accelerating frames, and then on every body in that frame.

steps.title: Problem 1: infinite ladder
steps.body:
Each section has R in series followed by R across (shunt). Let the equivalent resistance be X. Adding one section: X = R + (R·X)/(R + X).

⇒ X² − RX − R² = 0 ⇒ **X = R(1 + √5)/2 ≈ 1.618R**.

Pattern: self-similarity ⇒ set up 'X = f(X)'.

steps.title: Problem 2: RC charging
steps.body:
A 2 μF capacitor charges through 1 MΩ from a 10 V battery.
- Time constant τ = RC = 2 s.
- q(t) = CV(1 − e^{−t/τ}); current i = (V/R)e^{−t/τ}.
- Time to reach half charge: 1 − e^{−t/τ} = ½ ⇒ t = τ ln 2 ≈ **1.39 s**.
- At t = τ: charge ≈ 63% of maximum.
- Energy: the battery supplies CV²; half is stored (½CV²) and half is dissipated in R—independent of R!

steps.title: Problem 3: arcs and crossed fields
steps.body:
(a) Field at the centre of a semicircular arc (radius R, current I): half of a full loop ⇒ **B = μ₀I/(4R)**. The straight leads pointing radially contribute zero (dl ∥ r).

(b) A charged particle passes undeflected through perpendicular E and B: qE = qvB ⇒ **v = E/B** (a velocity selector). If E is then switched off, the particle circles with r = mv/(qB).

steps.title: Problem 4: terminal velocity of a sliding rod
steps.body:
A rod of length l and mass m slides on frictionless rails joined by resistance R, in a vertical field B; a constant force F pulls it.
- EMF = Blv; current I = Blv/R; magnetic force = BIl = B²l²v/R opposing motion.
- m dv/dt = F − B²l²v/R ⇒ terminal **v_t = FR/(B²l²)**, approached exponentially with time constant mR/(B²l²).
- At terminal speed, power F·v_t = I²R—all work becomes heat ✔.

steps.title: Speed tricks
steps.body:
- Symmetry: points at equal potential can be joined or a resistor between them removed.
- In steady state DC, capacitors carry no current; inductors act like wires.
- Just after switching: uncharged capacitor acts like a wire; inductor like a break.
- Check limiting cases: R → 0, R → ∞.

steps.title: SHM toolkit
steps.body:
- SHM: a = −ω²x; x = A sin(ωt + φ); v = ω√(A² − x²); a_max = ω²A; total energy ½kA².
- Spring–mass: T = 2π√(m/k). Springs in parallel: k = k₁ + k₂; in series: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂.
- Simple pendulum: T = 2π√(L/g_eff). In a lift accelerating up at a: g_eff = g + a ⇒ the clock runs **fast**; in free fall T → ∞.

steps.title: Problem 1: spring combinations
steps.body:
A 1 kg mass hangs from two identical springs (k = 200 N/m each).
- In parallel: k = 400 ⇒ T = 2π√(1/400) = π/10 ≈ 0.314 s.
- In series: k = 100 ⇒ T = 2π/10 ≈ 0.628 s.
Cutting a spring in half doubles its k.

steps.title: Waves on strings and in pipes
steps.body:
- Wave speed on a string: **v = √(T/μ)** (μ = mass per unit length).
- String fixed at both ends / pipe open at both ends: fₙ = nv/(2L) (all harmonics).
- Pipe closed at one end: f = (2n − 1)v/(4L) (odd harmonics only).
- Beats: f_beat = |f₁ − f₂|.
- Doppler (sound, source and observer on a line): f' = f(v + v_o)/(v − v_s) for approach.

steps.title: Problem 2: pipes and beats
steps.body:
An open pipe of length 0.5 m and a closed pipe sound their fundamentals; v = 340 m/s.
- Open: f = v/2L = 340 Hz.
- A closed pipe giving the same fundamental needs L = v/(4f) = 0.25 m.
- If the closed pipe is 0.26 m: f = 340/1.04 ≈ 326.9 Hz ⇒ beats ≈ 13 per second.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Using total length instead of mass per unit length in √(T/μ).
- Forgetting that closed pipes lack even harmonics.
- Mixing angular frequency ω (rad/s) with frequency f (Hz): ω = 2πf.

steps.title: Problem 1: photoelectric with two wavelengths
steps.body:
A metal gives stopping potential 1.85 V with 300 nm light. Find φ and the stopping potential for 400 nm.
- E₁ = 1240/300 ≈ 4.13 eV ⇒ φ = 4.13 − 1.85 ≈ **2.28 eV**.
- E₂ = 1240/400 = 3.10 eV ⇒ V₀ = 3.10 − 2.28 ≈ **0.82 V**.

steps.title: Problem 2: hydrogen-like ions
steps.body:
Energy of the photon for Li²⁺ (Z = 3), n = 3 → n = 1:
ΔE = 13.6 × 9 × (1 − 1/9) = 13.6 × 8 = **108.8 eV**.

Radius ratio r(He⁺, n = 2)/r(H, n = 1) = (n²/Z) = 4/2 = 2.

steps.title: Problem 3: two radioactive samples
steps.body:
A (T½ = 2 h) and B (T½ = 4 h) start with equal numbers of nuclei. After 8 h: N_A = N₀/16, N_B = N₀/4 ⇒ **N_A/N_B = 1/4**.

Activity ratio: R = λN ⇒ R_A/R_B = (λ_A/λ_B)(N_A/N_B) = 2 × ¼ = **½**.

steps.title: Problem 4: slab shift and YDSE film
steps.body:
(a) A glass slab (t = 6 cm, n = 1.5) shifts an object (seen normally) by t(1 − 1/n) = 6 × (1/3) = **2 cm** towards the viewer.

(b) In YDSE, covering one slit with a film of thickness t and index n shifts the pattern by (n − 1)tD/d towards that slit. With n = 1.5, t = 6 μm, D = 1 m, d = 1 mm: shift = 0.5 × 6×10⁻⁶ × 10³ = **3 mm**.

steps.body:
- hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm; 1 u ≈ 931.5 MeV.
- Electron λ (nm) ≈ 1.227/√V.
- After n half-lives: (½)ⁿ; T½ = 0.693/λ.
- Ionisation energy of hydrogen-like ion = 13.6Z² eV.

steps.title: Problem 1: colligative properties
steps.body:
Freezing-point depression ΔT_f = i K_f m.
- 0.1 m NaCl (i ≈ 2), K_f(water) = 1.86 K kg/mol ⇒ ΔT_f ≈ 0.372 K.
- 0.1 m glucose (i = 1) ⇒ 0.186 K.
Salt gives twice the effect per mole because it dissociates into two ions—one reason it's used on icy roads.

Osmotic pressure π = iCRT: 0.1 M glucose at 300 K ⇒ π = 0.1 × 0.0821 × 300 ≈ **2.46 atm**.

steps.title: Problem 2: quantum numbers and nodes
steps.body:
- Radial nodes = n − l − 1; angular nodes = l; total = n − 1.
- 3p: n = 3, l = 1 ⇒ 1 radial node, 1 angular node.
- 4d: 1 radial, 2 angular.
- Maximum electrons with n = 3: 2n² = 18; with n = 3, l = 2: 10.
- (n + l) rule: 4s (4 + 0) fills before 3d (3 + 2).

steps.title: Problem 3: degree of dissociation
steps.body:
PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂ at total pressure P, degree of dissociation α.
- Moles: (1 − α), α, α; total (1 + α).
- K_p = [α/(1 + α)]²P² / [((1 − α)/(1 + α))P] = **α²P/(1 − α²)**.
- If α = 0.5 at P = 3 atm: K_p = 0.25 × 3/0.75 = **1 atm**.

steps.title: Problem 4: Raoult's law
steps.body:
Relative lowering of vapour pressure = mole fraction of solute (non-volatile, non-electrolyte).

10 g of a solute in 90 g water lowers vapour pressure by 2%. Mole fraction of solute 0.02 ⇒ n_solute/(n_solute + 5) = 0.02 ⇒ n ≈ 0.102 mol ⇒ molar mass ≈ 10/0.102 ≈ **98 g/mol**. (Approximation x ≈ n/n_water gives 0.1 mol, 100 g/mol.)

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Forgetting i for electrolytes (and that association, e.g., acetic acid in benzene, gives i < 1).
- Using molarity where molality is required.
- Using total moles instead of gaseous moles in K_p.

steps.title: Aromaticity (Hückel)
steps.body:
Aromatic if cyclic, planar, fully conjugated and has **(4n + 2) π electrons**.
- Benzene (6) ✔; cyclopentadienyl anion (6) ✔; tropylium (cycloheptatrienyl) cation (6) ✔; pyridine and pyrrole (6) ✔.
- Cyclobutadiene (4): antiaromatic. Cyclooctatetraene (8): non-planar tub ⇒ non-aromatic.

This explains why cyclopentadiene is unusually acidic (its anion is aromatic).

steps.title: Problem 1: Grignard and ozonolysis
steps.body:
(a) CH₃MgBr + acetone, then H₃O⁺ ⇒ (CH₃)₃COH, **2-methylpropan-2-ol** (a 3° alcohol). Grignard + HCHO ⇒ 1°; + other aldehydes ⇒ 2°; + ketones ⇒ 3°; + CO₂ ⇒ carboxylic acid.

(b) Ozonolysis (O₃ then Zn/H₂O) of but-2-ene ⇒ **2 CH₃CHO**. Of 2-methylbut-2-ene ⇒ acetone + ethanal. Read the products backwards to locate the C=C.

steps.title: Problem 2: carbon-count changers
steps.body:
- **Hofmann bromamide**: RCONH₂ + Br₂ + NaOH ⇒ RNH₂ (one carbon fewer).
- **Decarboxylation** (soda lime): RCOONa ⇒ RH (one carbon fewer).
- **Kolbe electrolysis**: 2RCOO⁻ ⇒ R–R (carbon chain doubles, minus CO₂).
- **Grignard + CO₂** or **nitrile hydrolysis** (R–X → R–CN → RCOOH) ⇒ one carbon more.

Example: convert ethanoic acid to methanamine: CH₃COOH → CH₃CONH₂ → (Hofmann) CH₃NH₂.

steps.title: Problem 3: acidity and basicity orders
steps.body:
- Acidity: HC≡CH > CH₂=CH₂ > CH₃CH₃ (sp > sp² > sp³ carbon).
- Phenols: p-nitrophenol > phenol > p-cresol (electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity).
- Basicity in water: (C₂H₅)₂NH > (C₂H₅)₃N > C₂H₅NH₂ > NH₃ (for ethyl amines; note the order differs for methyl amines).
- Aniline is weaker than cyclohexylamine (lone pair delocalised into the ring); pyrrole is barely basic (its lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet).

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Calling every ring with alternating double bonds aromatic—check planarity and the electron count.
- Forgetting Grignard reagents are destroyed by water, alcohols and acids (any O–H or N–H).
- Applying the methyl-amine basicity order to ethyl amines.

steps.title: Problem 1: oxidation states from structure
steps.body:
Naive counting fails when peroxide (O–O) bonds exist.

steps.title: Problem 2: tricky shapes
steps.body:

- **ClF₃**: 3 bp + 2 lp ⇒ **T-shaped**.

- **XeO₃**: 3 bp + 1 lp ⇒ **pyramidal**.

Lone pairs in trigonal bipyramidal arrangements sit in equatorial positions.

steps.title: Problem 3: magnetism and isomer counts
steps.body:
- [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺: Fe²⁺ d⁶, weak field ⇒ 4 unpaired ⇒ μ ≈ 4.90 BM; [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻: low spin ⇒ 0 BM.

- [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺: cis (optically active, a pair of enantiomers) + trans ⇒ **3 stereoisomers**.

steps.title: Speed checks
steps.body:

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Putting lone pairs in axial positions of a trigonal bipyramid.

steps.title: Problem 1: concentration cell
steps.body:
Cu | Cu²⁺ (0.01 M) || Cu²⁺ (1 M) | Cu. E° = 0, n = 2.

E = (0.0591/2) log(1/0.01) = 0.0296 × 2 ≈ **0.059 V**. Electrons flow from the dilute side (anode) to the concentrated side (cathode) until concentrations equalise.

steps.title: Problem 2: Kohlrausch's law
steps.body:
Λ°m(CH₃COOH) = Λ°m(CH₃COONa) + Λ°m(HCl) − Λ°m(NaCl).

With 91, 426 and 126 S cm² mol⁻¹: Λ°m = 91 + 426 − 126 = **391 S cm² mol⁻¹**. If Λm at some concentration is 39.1, the degree of dissociation α = 39.1/391 = 0.1.

steps.title: Problem 3: kinetics
steps.body:
(a) For nth-order reactions, t½ ∝ [A]₀^(1 − n): doubling [A]₀ halves t½ for second order, leaves it unchanged for first order, and doubles it for zero order.

(b) Arrhenius: k doubles from 300 K to 310 K ⇒ E_a = 2.303R log 2 × (300 × 310/10) ≈ 2.303 × 8.314 × 0.301 × 9300 ≈ **53.6 kJ/mol**.

(c) A first-order reaction is 20% complete in 10 min: k = (2.303/10) log(1/0.8) ≈ 0.0223 min⁻¹ ⇒ t½ ≈ 31 min.

steps.title: Speed checks
steps.body:

- ΔG° = −nFE° ⇒ −96.5 kJ per mol of electrons per volt.
- log 2 ≈ 0.301, log 3 ≈ 0.477.
- Equal t½ regardless of [A]₀ is the fingerprint of first order.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Reversing anode and cathode in concentration cells.
- Forgetting to convert ΔG from J to kJ.
- Using log instead of ln without the 2.303 factor.

steps.title: Problem 1: root relations
steps.body:
For ax² + bx + c = 0: α + β = −b/a, αβ = c/a.
- x² − 5x + 6: α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 25 − 12 = **13**.
- α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β) = 125 − 90 = **35**.
- Both roots positive ⇔ discriminant ≥ 0, sum > 0, product > 0.

steps.title: Problem 2: cube roots of unity
steps.body:
ω³ = 1, 1 + ω + ω² = 0.
- (1 + ω)(1 + ω²) = 1 + ω + ω² + ω³ = 0 + 1 = **1**.
- (1 − ω + ω²)(1 + ω − ω²) = (−2ω)(−2ω²) = 4ω³ = **4**.
- |z₁ + z₂| ≤ |z₁| + |z₂| (triangle inequality); arg(z₁z₂) = arg z₁ + arg z₂ (mod 2π).

steps.title: Problem 3: binomial theorem
steps.body:
General term T_{r+1} = ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ.
- Coefficient of x⁴ in (1 + x)¹⁰: ¹⁰C₄ = **210**.
- Term independent of x in (x + 1/x)⁶: power of x is 6 − 2r = 0 ⇒ r = 3 ⇒ ⁶C₃ = **20**.
- Sum of coefficients: put x = 1. Sum of binomial coefficients ⁿC₀ + … + ⁿCₙ = 2ⁿ.

steps.title: Problem 4: AM–GM
steps.body:
For positive numbers, AM ≥ GM, equality when they are equal.
- Minimum of x + 4/x (x > 0): ≥ 2√4 = **4**, at x = 2.
- If a + b = 10 (a, b > 0), the maximum of ab is 25.
- Sum of a GP: a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); infinite GP with |r| < 1: a/(1 − r).

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Applying AM–GM to negative numbers.
- Forgetting T_{r+1} (not T_r) in the binomial general term.
- Using α + β = b/a (sign error).

scenes.text: Ishita stares at ∫₀^π x sin x dx. 'By parts works,' says her coach, 'but watch this.'
He replaces x with π − x, adds the two versions, and the x disappears.
Symmetry tricks turn ten-minute integrals into one-minute ones.

steps.title: Problem 1: limits with series
steps.body:
lim_{x→0} (x − sin x)/x³: sin x = x − x³/6 + … ⇒ (x³/6)/x³ = **1/6**.

lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1 − x)/x² = **½** (eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2 + …).

lim_{x→∞} (1 + 2/x)^x = **e²**.

Series expansions beat repeated L'Hôpital for 0/0 forms with higher powers.

steps.title: Problem 2: King's property
steps.body:
I = ∫₀^π x sin x dx. Replace x by π − x: I = ∫₀^π (π − x) sin x dx. Add: 2I = π∫₀^π sin x dx = 2π ⇒ **I = π**.

Classic: ∫₀^{π/2} ln(sin x) dx = **−(π/2) ln 2** (using the same property plus sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x).

steps.title: Problem 3: extrema and counting roots
steps.body:
f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 4. f'(x) = 3x(x − 2) ⇒ critical points 0 and 2. f(0) = 4 (local max), f(2) = 0 (local min).

So f(x) = 0 has a repeated root at x = 2 and one more root (f(−1) = 0 ⇒ x = −1). The number of real roots of f(x) = k is 3 for 0 < k < 4, 2 for k = 0 or 4, and 1 otherwise.

steps.title: Problem 4: area with modulus
steps.body: Area between y = |x| and y = 2 − x²: they meet where x = 2 − x² (x ≥ 0) ⇒ x = 1. By symmetry, A = 2∫₀¹ (2 − x² − x)dx = 2(2 − 1/3 − 1/2) = **7/3**.

steps.title: Trick list
steps.body:
- ∫₀^{2a} f(x)dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx if f(2a − x) = f(x); 0 if f(2a − x) = −f(x).
- Periodic f with period T: ∫₀^{nT} f = n∫₀^T f.
- Leibniz rule: d/dx ∫_{a(x)}^{b(x)} f(t)dt = f(b)b' − f(a)a'.
- Draw the graph before computing an area.

scenes.text: Tanmay's uncle installs a satellite dish on a rooftop in Bhubaneswar. 'The receiver must sit exactly at the focus,' he says.
Tanmay realises the dish is a parabola rotated about its axis.
Conics are pictures you can compute—and JEE loves them.

steps.title: Problem 1: lines and circles
steps.body:
- Distance from (1, 2) to 3x + 4y − 5 = 0: |3 + 8 − 5|/5 = **6/5**.
- x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 12 = 0: centre (2, −3), radius √(4 + 9 + 12) = **5**.
- A line is tangent to a circle iff its distance from the centre equals the radius.
- Two circles touch externally iff the distance between centres = r₁ + r₂; internally iff = |r₁ − r₂|.

steps.title: Problem 2: parabola
steps.body:
y² = 4ax: focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a, latus rectum 4a.
- y² = 8x: a = 2 ⇒ focus (2, 0), latus rectum **8**.
- Tangent of slope m: **y = mx + a/m**.
- Focal chord property: for a focal chord with ends at parameters t₁ and t₂, t₁t₂ = −1.
- Every ray parallel to the axis reflects through the focus (the dish!).

steps.title: Problem 3: ellipse and hyperbola
steps.body:
Ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a > b): b² = a²(1 − e²); foci (±ae, 0); sum of focal distances = 2a.
- x²/25 + y²/9 = 1: e = √(1 − 9/25) = **4/5**, foci (±4, 0).

Hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1: b² = a²(e² − 1); |difference of focal distances| = 2a; asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x. A rectangular hyperbola has e = √2.

steps.title: Speed tricks
steps.body:
- Parametric points: parabola (at², 2at); ellipse (a cos θ, b sin θ).
- Condition for y = mx + c to touch x²/a² + y²/b² = 1: c² = a²m² + b².
- Locus questions: let the point be (h, k), write conditions, eliminate parameters, replace h, k by x, y.

steps.body:

- Sign errors when completing the square for the centre.

steps.title: Problem 1: arrangements with repetition
steps.body:
Arrangements of MISSISSIPPI (11 letters: M1, I4, S4, P2): 11!/(4! 4! 2!) = **34,650**.

With the four I's together: treat IIII as one block ⇒ 8 items with S4, P2: 8!/(4! 2!) = **840**.

steps.title: Problem 3: distribution and selection
steps.body:
- Non-negative integer solutions of x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = 10: ¹²C₂ = **66** (stars and bars: ⁿ⁺ʳ⁻¹C_{r−1}).
- Positive integer solutions: ⁹C₂ = **36**.
- Committees of 5 from 6 men and 4 women with at least 2 women: ⁴C₂⁶C₃ + ⁴C₃⁶C₂ + ⁴C₄⁶C₁ = 120 + 60 + 6 = **186**.
- Circular arrangements of n distinct people: (n − 1)!.

steps.title: Problem 4: probability with conditions
steps.body:
A die is rolled until a 6 appears. Probability that it takes exactly 3 rolls: (5/6)²(1/6) = **25/216**.

Two cards are drawn without replacement. P(both aces) = (4/52)(3/51) = **1/221**.

Expected number of rolls to get a 6: 1/p = 6.

steps.body:
- Using permutations when order doesn't matter.
- Overcounting with 'at least' conditions—use complements or case-splitting cleanly.
- Forgetting that circular arrangements of beads (necklace) are further halved: (n − 1)!/2.

lessons.title: Planning and mock-test analysis

scenes.text: Two friends in Patna, Vivek and Saba, both study 8 hours a day for JEE.
Vivek re-reads notes and solves only problems he likes. Saba takes a weekly mock and spends three hours analysing every mistake.
By January, Saba's scores have risen steadily; Vivek's are flat. The difference is feedback.

steps.title: About this material
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide (information bulletin) for the current syllabus, pattern and marking scheme—these can change from year to year.

steps.title: A weekly rhythm
steps.body:
- Rotate subjects daily; each day include one new topic, one practice block and one revision block.
- Use **spaced revision**: revisit a topic after about 1 day, 1 week and 1 month.
- **Active recall** beats re-reading: close the book and write the derivation or formula from memory.
- One full-length mock every week (more in the final months), at the same time of day as the real exam.
- Protect 7–8 hours of sleep: memory consolidation happens during sleep.

steps.title: The error log
steps.body:
After each mock, classify every lost mark:
- **Concept gap** (didn't know) → revisit theory + 10 targeted problems.
- **Silly mistake** (sign, unit, misread) → note the pattern; add a check step.
- **Time** (knew it, ran out) → practise speed or skip earlier.
- **Guess gone wrong** → refine your guessing rule.
Review the log every Sunday. Repeated errors are your highest-value targets.

steps.title: Saba's analysis
steps.body: Mock score 150/300. Error log: 40 marks lost to concept gaps (mostly rotation and coordination compounds), 28 to silly mistakes (units in physics), 30 to time (stuck on two maths questions). Her next week: rotation + coordination theory, a 'units check' habit, and a rule to leave any question after 4 minutes. Next mock: 182.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Measuring hours instead of problems solved and errors fixed.
- Collecting too many books—finish one good source per subject thoroughly first.
- Comparing your mock ranks with friends daily; compare with your own last week.

activity.prompt: Your weekly mock routine
items: Take a full mock under timed, exam-like conditions
Mark every lost question: concept, silly, time or guess
Re-solve every wrong question without looking at the solution
Write the top 3 repeated errors on a sticky note

Sleep at least 7 hours the night before the mock

lessons.title: Inside the paper: time and negative marking

scenes.text: Meera used to start at Question 1 and fight every question in order. She often left easy questions at the end unattempted.
Her coach teaches a three-pass method: easy first, medium second, hard last.
And a little probability tells her exactly when guessing is worth it.

steps.title: Three passes
steps.body:
1. **Pass 1** (fast): answer everything you can do in under ~1–2 minutes with confidence.
2. **Pass 2**: return to questions you can do with more work.
3. **Pass 3**: attempt the hardest, or make calculated guesses where rules allow.
Mark question numbers on the rough sheet (✔ done, ○ later, ✕ skip) so you never lose track.

steps.title: Expected value of guessing
steps.body:
Suppose a question has 4 options with +4 for correct and −1 for wrong (always check the current marking scheme).
- Pure guess: EV = ¼(4) + ¾(−1) = **+0.25**—slightly positive.
- Eliminate 1 option: EV = ⅓(4) − ⅔(1) = **+2/3**.
- Eliminate 2 options: EV = ½(4) − ½(1) = **+1.5**.
For numerical-answer questions without options, a random guess has almost no chance and is usually wasted time—unless there is no negative marking.

EV is about averages over many questions; for one question, guess only when you've eliminated options.

steps.title: Time rules
steps.body:
- Set a per-question 'walk-away' time (for example, 4 minutes) and obey it.
- Keep the last 10 minutes for transferring/checking answers and unattempted easy items.
- Don't change answers without a clear reason; first instincts backed by working are usually better than panic switching.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Spending 15 minutes on one question to 'prove' you can.
- Guessing blindly on many questions when negative marking is heavy.
- Skipping the instructions page—marking schemes differ by section.

scenes.text: On exam morning in Lucknow, Ayaan's hands shake as he enters the centre. His mind goes blank on the first question.
He remembers a trick from a Mann wellbeing lesson: slow breathing with a longer out-breath.
Two minutes later, the first formula returns. Nerves are normal—and manageable.

steps.title: Why your mind goes blank
steps.body: Stress triggers adrenaline (fight-or-flight): heart races, breathing quickens and working memory narrows. A little arousal helps focus; too much blocks recall. You can deliberately turn it down.

steps.title: Two-minute reset
steps.body:
- Breathe in through the nose for 4, hold 4, out slowly for 4, hold 4 (box breathing)—or simply make the out-breath longer than the in-breath.
- Plant your feet, notice five things you can see.
- Tell yourself: 'This is adrenaline. It means I care. I'll start with the easiest question.'
- Then do exactly that—an easy win restores confidence.

steps.title: The days before
steps.body:
- No new topics in the last 2–3 days—revise your own notes and error log.
- Sleep at your usual time; caffeine late at night harms sleep.
- Keep admit card, ID and permitted items ready the night before; check the reporting time and route.
- Eat a familiar light meal; carry water if allowed.

steps.title: You are more than a rank
steps.body: Results matter, but they don't decide your worth. There are many good paths—other exams, other colleges, other years. If stress feels unbearable, if you can't sleep or eat for days, or if you have thoughts of harming yourself, talk to someone now: a parent, teacher or counsellor, Tele-MANAS **14416**, or **112** in an emergency. See the Mann (wellbeing) school for more.

steps.title: Enzymes in a nutshell
steps.body:
- Enzymes lower activation energy; most are proteins (ribozymes are catalytic RNA).
- Factors: temperature, pH, substrate concentration (rate levels off at saturation).
- **Competitive inhibition**: the inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site—e.g., **malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase**.
- Cofactors: prosthetic groups (tightly bound, e.g., haem), coenzymes (e.g., NAD, NADP—contain vitamins such as niacin), metal ions (e.g., Zn²⁺ in carboxypeptidase).
- Six classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases.

steps.title: High-yield genetic disorders
steps.body:
- **Sickle-cell anaemia**: autosomal recessive; GAG → GUG in the β-globin gene ⇒ glutamic acid replaced by valine at the 6th position.
- **Thalassaemia**: autosomal recessive; reduced synthesis of α or β globin chains (a quantitative problem).
- **Phenylketonuria**: autosomal recessive; phenylalanine can't be converted to tyrosine.
- **Haemophilia, colour blindness**: X-linked recessive.
- **Down syndrome**: trisomy 21 (47 chromosomes). **Turner syndrome**: 45, XO (female). **Klinefelter syndrome**: 47, XXY (male).

steps.title: Drill: pedigree reasoning
steps.body: Two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. The trait must be **autosomal recessive**: if it were X-linked recessive, her father would have to be affected. Each further child has a 1/4 chance of being affected; an unaffected sibling has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Sickle-cell is a qualitative defect (wrong amino acid); thalassaemia is quantitative (too little globin).
- Turner syndrome has 45 chromosomes, not 47.
- Competitive inhibitors can be overcome by more substrate; non-competitive ones cannot.

scenes.text: In western Uttar Pradesh, farmer Gurnam grows wheat in winter and sugarcane in the hot season.
His nephew Aman, preparing for NEET, learns that sugarcane is a C₄ plant—built to photosynthesise efficiently in heat and bright light.
Wheat, a C₃ plant, wastes some energy on photorespiration on hot days.

steps.title: Light reactions
steps.body:
- **PS II** (reaction centre P680) and **PS I** (P700) in the thylakoid membranes.
- **Photolysis of water** at PS II releases O₂—the O₂ comes from water, not CO₂ (shown with the ¹⁸O isotope).
- Non-cyclic photophosphorylation makes ATP and NADPH; cyclic (PS I only) makes ATP only.
- ATP synthesis is by chemiosmosis: protons build up in the thylakoid lumen and flow out through ATP synthase.

steps.title: Calvin cycle and C₄ plants
steps.body:
- Calvin cycle (stroma): **RuBisCO** fixes CO₂ onto RuBP ⇒ 3-PGA (first stable product of C₃ plants). Each CO₂ needs 3 ATP + 2 NADPH; one glucose needs 18 ATP and 12 NADPH (6 turns).
- **Photorespiration** (C₃ plants, high O₂/high temperature): RuBisCO binds O₂ instead, wasting energy.
- **C₄ plants** (maize, sugarcane, sorghum): **Kranz anatomy**; PEP carboxylase in mesophyll fixes CO₂ into oxaloacetate (first product, 4-carbon); CO₂ is released in bundle-sheath cells for the Calvin cycle ⇒ little photorespiration.

steps.title: Respiration
steps.body:
- **Glycolysis** (cytoplasm): glucose → 2 pyruvate; net 2 ATP + 2 NADH.
- Link reaction: pyruvate → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ (+ NADH).
- **Krebs cycle** (mitochondrial matrix), per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP (GTP), 2 CO₂.
- ETS and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner membrane; O₂ is the final electron acceptor.
- NCERT's theoretical net yield: 38 ATP per glucose (actual cell yields are lower).
- **Respiratory quotient** RQ = CO₂ released/O₂ used: carbohydrates 1; fats about 0.7; proteins about 0.9; anaerobic respiration: infinite (no O₂ used).

steps.title: Plant growth regulators
steps.body:
- **Auxins** (IAA): apical dominance, rooting of cuttings, parthenocarpy; 2,4-D as a weedkiller for dicot weeds.
- **Gibberellins**: stem elongation, bolting, increase sugarcane yield, speed up malting.
- **Cytokinins**: cell division, delay leaf senescence, overcome apical dominance.
- **Ethylene** (a gas): fruit ripening, abscission; ethephon releases ethylene.
- **Abscisic acid**: stress hormone—stomatal closure, seed dormancy.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- The first stable product in C₄ plants is oxaloacetate (OAA), not 3-PGA.
- O₂ in photosynthesis comes from water.
- Gibberellins, not auxins, cause bolting in rosette plants.

story.title: The numbers that keep you alive

scenes.text: Mansi, a NEET repeater in Indore, keeps losing marks on physiology numbers and hormone sources.
Her mentor gives her a one-page 'numbers and sources' sheet and drills it daily for a week.
Her physiology accuracy goes from 60% to 90%.

steps.title: Numbers worth knowing
steps.body:
- Tidal volume ≈ 500 mL; vital capacity ≈ 3.5–4.5 L; residual volume ≈ 1.1–1.2 L.
- Cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min; cardiac cycle ≈ 0.8 s at 72/min.
- GFR ≈ 125 mL/min (≈ 180 L/day); urine ≈ 1.5 L/day.
- Normal adult BP ≈ 120/80 mmHg.
- Resting membrane potential ≈ −70 mV.
- RBC lifespan ≈ 120 days; haemoglobin ≈ 12–16 g per 100 mL blood.

steps.title: Where hormones come from
steps.body:
- Hypothalamus: releasing/inhibiting hormones; makes oxytocin and ADH (stored in the posterior pituitary).
- Anterior pituitary: GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin.
- Thyroid: T₃, T₄, calcitonin; parathyroid: PTH (raises blood Ca²⁺).
- Adrenal cortex: cortisol, aldosterone; adrenal medulla: adrenaline, noradrenaline.
- Pancreas: insulin (β), glucagon (α).
- Heart atrium: ANF; kidney: erythropoietin; GI tract: gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP.

steps.title: Muscle and movement
steps.body:
- Sliding filament theory: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, exposing myosin-binding sites on actin; myosin heads (using ATP) pull actin.
- During contraction, the I-band and H-zone shorten; the A-band stays the same length.
- Gout: uric acid crystals in joints; myasthenia gravis: autoimmune, affects the neuromuscular junction; osteoporosis: reduced bone mass (low oestrogen is a factor).

steps.title: Drill: integrate two systems
steps.body:
A person loses a lot of blood. What happens?
- BP falls ⇒ juxtaglomerular cells release **renin** ⇒ angiotensin II ⇒ vasoconstriction + **aldosterone** (Na⁺ and water retention).
- ADH rises ⇒ more water reabsorbed.
- Over days, kidneys release more **erythropoietin** ⇒ more RBCs.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- ADH and oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus, not the pituitary.
- The A-band does not shorten during contraction.
- PTH raises blood calcium; calcitonin lowers it.

scenes.text: During the monsoon in Mumbai, Dr Ansari's clinic is full of fever patients—malaria, dengue, typhoid.
Her intern Ritu must match each disease to its cause, carrier and test.
These matches are among the most frequently tested facts in NEET biology.

steps.title: Diseases: cause, carrier, clue
steps.body:
- **Malaria**: *Plasmodium* (protozoan); spread by the **female *Anopheles*** mosquito; recurring chills and high fever linked to release of haemozoin.
- **Typhoid**: *Salmonella typhi* (bacterium); contaminated food/water; confirmed by the **Widal test**.
- **Pneumonia**: *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*.
- **Dengue and chikungunya**: viruses spread by *Aedes* mosquitoes.
- **Filariasis (elephantiasis)**: *Wuchereria* worms spread by *Culex*.
- **Ascariasis**: roundworm *Ascaris*; **amoebiasis**: *Entamoeba histolytica* (houseflies are mechanical carriers).
- **Ringworm**: fungi (*Microsporum*, *Trichophyton*, *Epidermophyton*).

steps.title: Immunity
steps.body:
- Innate (barriers, phagocytes, fever) vs acquired (B cells → antibodies; T cells → cell-mediated).
- Antibody classes: IgA (in colostrum and secretions), IgG (crosses the placenta), IgE (allergy), IgM (first made), IgD.
- Active immunity: vaccines or infection (slow, long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies (fast, short-lived)—e.g., antitoxins for snakebite.
- **HIV** is a retrovirus that infects helper T (CD4) cells; diagnosed by ELISA; managed with antiretroviral therapy.

steps.title: Reproduction recap
steps.body:
- Spermatogenesis: 1 primary spermatocyte → 4 sperm; oogenesis: 1 primary oocyte → 1 ovum + polar bodies.
- LH surge triggers ovulation (about mid-cycle); corpus luteum secretes progesterone.
- Fertilisation in the ampulla; implantation of the blastocyst; hCG maintains the corpus luteum.
- Contraceptives: barrier (condoms also reduce STI risk), IUDs (copper ions reduce sperm motility), oral pills (inhibit ovulation), surgical methods.
- ART: IVF with embryo transfer (ZIFT, IUT), GIFT, ICSI, IUI.

steps.title: Biotechnology recap
steps.body:
- EcoRI recognises GAATTC; DNA ligase joins; pBR322 has ampicillin and tetracycline resistance genes; insertional inactivation with the β-galactosidase gene gives blue–white screening.
- PCR: denaturation → annealing → extension (Taq polymerase).
- Bt cotton (cry genes); RNAi against *Meloidogyne incognita* in tobacco; recombinant insulin (A and B chains made separately and joined); first clinical gene therapy for ADA deficiency (1990).

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Malaria is spread by the female *Anopheles*; dengue by *Aedes*; filariasis by *Culex*.
- IgA is in colostrum; IgG crosses the placenta.
- Copper-T acts by releasing Cu²⁺ ions, not by blocking ovulation.

lessons.title: Evolution and ecology: concepts and calculations

scenes.text: Student Kabir reads about peppered moths in industrial England: as soot darkened tree trunks, dark moths became common.
When pollution fell, light moths returned.
His teacher turns it into a Hardy–Weinberg problem.

steps.title: Evolution essentials
steps.body:
- **Natural selection** (Darwin, Wallace): variation + inheritance + overproduction + differential survival.
- Evidence: fossils, homologous organs (same origin, different function—forelimbs of whales, bats, humans: divergent evolution), analogous organs (different origin, similar function—wings of birds and insects: convergent evolution).
- **Industrial melanism** (peppered moth) and antibiotic or pesticide resistance are examples of selection.
- Miller–Urey (1953): electric discharge in a mixture of CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and water vapour produced amino acids.

steps.title: Hardy–Weinberg drills
steps.body:
p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (no mutation, migration, selection, drift; random mating).

If 16% of a population shows a recessive phenotype: q² = 0.16 ⇒ q = 0.4, p = 0.6. Carriers 2pq = **0.48 (48%)**; homozygous dominant p² = 0.36.

Factors that disturb equilibrium: gene flow, genetic drift (founder effect), mutation, genetic recombination, natural selection.

steps.title: Population interactions
steps.body:
- Mutualism (+/+): lichens, mycorrhizae, fig and wasp.
- Commensalism (+/0): orchid on a mango branch; barnacles on whales; cattle egret and grazing cattle.
- Parasitism (+/−): tapeworm, Cuscuta on plants. Brood parasitism: the koel lays eggs in a crow's nest.
- Amensalism (0/−), competition (−/−), predation (+/−).
- Growth: exponential dN/dt = rN; logistic dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), K = carrying capacity.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Homologous ⇒ divergent evolution; analogous ⇒ convergent evolution.
- 2pq is the carrier frequency, not q².
- Orchid on a mango tree is commensalism (it is an epiphyte, not a parasite).

scenes.text: Many NEET aspirants, like Zara in Srinagar, fear physics most. She loves biology and memorises well, but physics numericals slow her down.
Her mentor gives her a one-page formula sheet and 20 problems a day, sorted by pattern.
In six weeks, Zara recognises most problems on sight.

steps.title: About this material
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.

steps.title: Pattern sheet: mechanics
steps.body:
- Equations of motion; projectile T = 2u sin θ/g, H = u² sin²θ/2g, R = u² sin 2θ/g.
- Work–energy theorem: W_net = ΔKE. Power P = Fv.
- Elastic collision of equal masses: velocities exchange.
- Momentum–KE: KE = p²/2m (same momentum ⇒ lighter body has more KE).
- Rotational: τ = Iα, L = Iω, rolling KE = ½mv²(1 + k²/R²).

steps.title: Gravitation
steps.body:
- g at height h (h ≪ R): g' ≈ g(1 − 2h/R); at depth d: g' = g(1 − d/R); g = 0 at the centre.
- Escape velocity v_e = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s for Earth; orbital velocity near the surface v_o = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s; v_e = √2 v_o.
- Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³. Geostationary satellites: period 24 h, about 36 000 km above the equator.
- Gravitational PE U = −GMm/r; total energy of an orbit = −GMm/2r.

steps.title: Drills
steps.body:
1) A satellite's orbital radius is made 4 times larger. Its period becomes 4^{3/2} = **8 times**.
2) Two bodies have equal KE, masses 1 kg and 4 kg. Momentum ratio p₁ : p₂ = √1 : √4 = **1 : 2**.
3) At what height is g reduced by 1%? 2h/R = 0.01 ⇒ h = R/200 ≈ **32 km**.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Escape velocity does not depend on the mass of the escaping body or the direction of launch.
- g' ≈ g(1 − 2h/R) works only for h ≪ R; otherwise use g' = g R²/(R + h)².
- Weightlessness in orbit is not 'zero gravity'—it is continuous free fall.

scenes.text: Ravi connects a 100 W and a 60 W bulb (both rated 220 V) in series. To his surprise, the 60 W bulb glows brighter.
In parallel, the 100 W bulb is brighter. 'How can both be true?' he asks.
Resistance is the key—a classic NEET question.

steps.title: Drill 1: bulbs in series and parallel
steps.body:
R = V²/P: 100 W bulb R = 484 Ω; 60 W bulb R ≈ 807 Ω.
- **Series** (same current): P = I²R ⇒ the larger R (60 W bulb) glows brighter.
- **Parallel** (same voltage): P = V²/R ⇒ the smaller R (100 W bulb) glows brighter.

steps.title: Drill 2: capacitors and cells
steps.body:
- Two capacitors C and 2C in series across V: charge Q = (2C/3)V; voltage across C is 2V/3.
- n identical cells (E, r) in series with external R: I = nE/(R + nr). In parallel: I = E/(R + r/n).
- Potentiometer: compares EMFs without drawing current at balance: E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂.

steps.title: Drill 3: magnetic quick facts
steps.body:
- Field at the centre of a circular coil: μ₀NI/2R. At the centre of a semicircle: μ₀I/4R.
- Radius of a charged particle: r = mv/qB = √(2mK)/qB. For the same K, a proton and an α-particle have radii in ratio 1 : 1 (√(m)/q: √1/1 vs √4/2).
- Magnetic materials: diamagnetic (χ small, negative; e.g., bismuth, water), paramagnetic (small positive; e.g., aluminium), ferromagnetic (large positive; e.g., iron, nickel, cobalt).

steps.title: EMI and AC quick facts
steps.body:
- ε = −dΦ/dt; Lenz's law.
- V_rms = V₀/√2; resonance ω = 1/√(LC); at resonance the power factor is 1.
- Transformer: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p.
- In a pure capacitor, current leads voltage by 90°; in a pure inductor it lags by 90°.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Assuming the higher-wattage bulb is always brighter.
- Mixing radius formulas for equal speed vs equal kinetic energy.
- Forgetting that a capacitor blocks steady DC.

Almost every NEET modern-physics topic sits inside that one device.

steps.title: Optics quick facts
steps.body:
- Lens: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f; P = 1/f (m). Mirror: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.
- Prism minimum deviation: n = sin[(A + δm)/2]/sin(A/2). Thin prism: δ = (n − 1)A.
- Compound microscope magnification ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e); telescope (normal adjustment) m = f_o/f_e.
- YDSE fringe width β = λD/d; Malus I = I₀cos²θ.

steps.title: Modern physics quick facts
steps.body:
- E (eV) = 1240/λ (nm); K_max = hν − φ.
- Hydrogen: Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV; Lyman (UV), Balmer (visible), Paschen (IR).
- Nucleus: R = R₀A^{1/3}; binding energy per nucleon peaks near Fe.
- Decay: N = N₀(½)^{t/T½}; α: A − 4, Z − 2; β⁻: Z + 1.

steps.title: Semiconductors
steps.body:
- Intrinsic: pure Si/Ge. n-type: doped with pentavalent atoms (P, As)—majority carriers electrons. p-type: trivalent (B, Al, In)—majority carriers holes.
- p–n junction: forward bias narrows the depletion layer (current flows); reverse bias widens it.
- Zener diode: used in reverse breakdown as a voltage regulator. LEDs emit light in forward bias; photodiodes work in reverse bias.
- Logic gates: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR. **NAND and NOR are universal gates.** NAND output is 0 only when all inputs are 1.

steps.title: Reagent map
steps.body:
- **PCC**: 1° alcohol → aldehyde. **KMnO₄ / K₂Cr₂O₇ (acid)**: 1° alcohol → acid; 2° → ketone.
- **LiAlH₄**: reduces acids, esters, aldehydes, ketones to alcohols; amides and nitriles to amines. **NaBH₄**: aldehydes and ketones only.
- **Zn–Hg/HCl (Clemmensen)** or **NH₂NH₂/KOH (Wolff–Kishner)**: C=O → CH₂.
- **Lindlar's catalyst**: alkyne → cis-alkene. **Na in liquid NH₃**: alkyne → trans-alkene.
- **Alcoholic KOH**: elimination; **aqueous KOH**: substitution.

steps.title: Named reactions to know
steps.body:
- **Reimer–Tiemann**: phenol + CHCl₃ + NaOH → salicylaldehyde.
- **Kolbe's reaction**: sodium phenoxide + CO₂ → salicylic acid.
- **Sandmeyer**: diazonium salt + CuCl/CuBr/CuCN → aryl halide/nitrile.
- **Gattermann–Koch**: benzene + CO + HCl (AlCl₃/CuCl) → benzaldehyde.
- **Etard**: toluene + CrO₂Cl₂ → benzaldehyde.
- **Wurtz**: 2RX + 2Na → R–R. **Friedel–Crafts**: alkylation/acylation with AlCl₃.
- **Aldol, Cannizzaro, Hofmann bromamide, Gabriel phthalimide** (1° amines only).

steps.title: Drills
steps.body:
1) CH₃CH₂CN + LiAlH₄ ⇒ **CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂** (propan-1-amine).
2) Benzene diazonium chloride + CuCN ⇒ **benzonitrile**.
3) Acetophenone + Zn–Hg/HCl ⇒ **ethylbenzene**.
4) But-2-yne + Lindlar ⇒ **cis-but-2-ene**.

steps.title: Biomolecules and polymers (high-yield)
steps.body:
- Glucose: aldohexose; fructose: ketohexose; sucrose: non-reducing (glycosidic bond between C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose); maltose and lactose: reducing.
- Vitamins: B and C are water-soluble; A, D, E, K fat-soluble. Deficiencies: A – night blindness; D – rickets; C – scurvy; B₁ – beriberi; B₁₂ – pernicious anaemia; K – delayed clotting.
- Polymers: nylon-6,6 (hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid); Bakelite (phenol + formaldehyde); natural rubber is cis-polyisoprene; PHBV is biodegradable.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- NaBH₄ does not reduce carboxylic acids or esters (under normal conditions).
- Gabriel synthesis cannot make aromatic primary amines like aniline.
- Sucrose is non-reducing even though its parts are reducing sugars.

steps.title: Exceptions page
steps.body:
- Ionisation enthalpy: Be > B, Mg > Al, N > O.
- Electron gain enthalpy: Cl most negative (not F); noble gases positive.
- Bond dissociation enthalpy: Cl₂ > Br₂ > F₂ > I₂ (F₂ is unusually weak).
- Ga is smaller than Al (poor shielding by d electrons).
- Lanthanoid contraction: Zr ≈ Hf.
- Li forms a normal oxide, Na a peroxide, K/Rb/Cs superoxides on burning in air.

steps.title: Bonding quick table
steps.body:
- sp: BeCl₂ (linear); sp²: BF₃ (trigonal planar); sp³: CH₄, NH₃ (pyramidal), H₂O (bent).
- sp³d: PCl₅ (trigonal bipyramidal), SF₄ (see-saw), ClF₃ (T), XeF₂ (linear).
- sp³d²: SF₆ (octahedral), BrF₅ (square pyramidal), XeF₄ (square planar).
- MO: O₂ paramagnetic (bond order 2); N₂ bond order 3; B₂ paramagnetic.

steps.title: Coordination quick facts
steps.body:
- Werner's theory: primary valence = oxidation state; secondary valence = coordination number.
- [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ square planar, diamagnetic; [NiCl₄]²⁻ tetrahedral, paramagnetic; [Ni(CO)₄] tetrahedral, diamagnetic.
- EDTA (hexadentate) is used to treat lead poisoning and to estimate water hardness; cisplatin is an anticancer drug; haemoglobin contains Fe, chlorophyll contains Mg, vitamin B₁₂ contains Co.

steps.body:
1) Number of ions from [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ in water: [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ ⇒ **3 ions**; with AgNO₃ it gives **2 mol AgCl** per mole.
2) Magnetic moment of Cu²⁺ (d⁹): 1 unpaired ⇒ **1.73 BM**.
3) The element in chlorophyll: **Mg**.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Only chloride ions outside the coordination sphere precipitate with AgNO₃.
- F₂ has a lower bond enthalpy than Cl₂ and Br₂.
- Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰) compounds are generally colourless and diamagnetic.

steps.title: About this material
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current syllabus, pattern and marking scheme.

steps.title: Line-by-line method
steps.body:
1. Read a section once for understanding.
2. Close the book; write or say everything you remember (active recall).
3. Compare; underline what you missed—those lines are your revision list.
4. Turn diagrams into blank sketches and label them from memory.
5. Convert each table (diseases, hormones, enzymes) into flashcards.
6. Revisit after 1 day, 1 week and 1 month (spacing).

steps.title: Practice with purpose
steps.body:
- Do topic-wise question sets right after studying a chapter; then mixed sets weekly (interleaving).
- Keep an error log: concept gap, misread, careless, time.
- Biology: precision with terms; Physics: daily numericals; Chemistry: reactions + numericals + NCERT inorganic facts.
- Previous years' papers show style and emphasis; always cross-check against the current official syllabus.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Re-reading without testing yourself (it feels productive but builds little memory).
- Using too many sources before mastering one.
- Ignoring physics because it feels hard—small daily practice beats occasional marathons.

steps.title: Answer-sheet discipline
steps.body:
- Check the question number before every mark.
- Mark in blocks (e.g., every 5–10 questions) rather than all at the end—but never leave marking to the last two minutes.
- Use the pen type and marking style the instructions require; stray marks can cause errors.
- Fill roll number and booklet details carefully first.

steps.title: Guessing with negative marking
steps.body:
Assume +4 correct, −1 wrong, 4 options (always check the current scheme).
- Pure guess EV = ¼ × 4 − ¾ × 1 = +0.25.
- Eliminate two options ⇒ EV = +1.5.
So guess only after eliminating options; avoid blind guessing on many questions—the variance can hurt.

scenes.text: Fatima's family in Moradabad has high hopes for her NEET result. She stops sleeping well and skips meals.
Her cousin notices and encourages her to call Tele-MANAS. Talking helps more than she expected.
She learns that wellbeing isn't a distraction from preparation—it's part of it.

steps.title: Signs stress is too high
steps.body: Trouble sleeping most nights, loss of appetite, constant headaches or stomach aches, feeling hopeless, crying often, withdrawing from everyone, or being unable to study at all. These are signals to slow down and talk to someone—not signs of weakness.

steps.title: Daily protectors
steps.body:
- 7–8 hours of sleep; a 20–30 minute walk or exercise.
- Short breaks (e.g., 5 minutes every 25–50 minutes).
- Regular meals and water.
- One conversation a day with a friend or family member that isn't about exams.
- Limit doom-scrolling of toppers' stories and rank predictions.

steps.title: When to get help right away
steps.body: If you feel overwhelmed, hopeless, or have thoughts of harming yourself, please talk to someone today: a parent, teacher, counsellor or doctor; **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7); or **112** in an emergency. If a friend says such things, stay with them and help them reach help. More support is in the Mann (wellbeing) school.

steps.title: Many paths
steps.body: Medicine can be reached in more than one attempt or route, and there are many meaningful health careers—nursing, pharmacy, physiotherapy, public health, biomedical research, allied health sciences and more. Your worth is not a rank.
